title: the birth of the cousins
hook: King Pandu, out hunting, shoots a deer that turns out to be a sage, and the dying sage's curse shuts the door on his sons
carry: you've killed me in a moment of love

segments.voice: Yesterday, the crown went to Pandu, and Gandhari bound her eyes. A strip of cloth, folded and tied.

A stag and a doe, together in a quiet forest clearing. A king on the hunt sees them through the trees, draws his bow, and shoots, quickly, without warning. The arrows strike the stag, and it falls. Then, lying in the grass, it speaks in a man's voice. King Pandu has just shot a sage.
screen: `A STAG AND A DOE.` → `THE ARROWS STRIKE.` → `THE DEER SPEAKS.`

segments.voice: Back up a little. Pandu has had a good reign. At her self-choice, the princess Kunti, adopted daughter of King Kuntibhoja, chose Pandu for her husband. Bhishma also brought him a second wife, Madri, sister of the king of the Madras. Pandu won wars and filled the treasury. Then he went to live in the forest with both wives, and spent his days hunting. That's where he meets the deer. The stag is a sage named Kindama, who had taken a deer's form to be with his wife. As he dies, he says: even a king who hunts should not strike creatures in a moment like this. You've killed me in a moment of love. So hear this: when you go to your wife in love, you will die. And he dies. Pandu is undone. He grieves for the sage, and for himself: a king with no son, who now can never father one. So he gives up the royal life entirely, to live as an ascetic, begging, fasting, with no home. He gives his jewels and royal robes to Brahmanas, and sends his attendants back to Hastinapura with the news. Kunti and Madri refuse to go back; they'll practice austerities beside him. Notice the turn. Yesterday the crown passed over the blind brother. Today the crowned king sits in a forest, unable to have heirs, while Dhritarashtra and Gandhari remain in the palace. The story has quietly tipped, and Pandu begins to ask how the line can go on without him.
screen: `KUNTI AND MADRI.` · `A KING GOES TO THE FOREST.` · `KINDAMA'S CURSE.` · `A KING WITH NO HEIRS.`

segments.voice: Pandu's arrow left the bow in an instant, and the curse lasted the rest of his life. Bring to mind one quick action of yours that had long consequences, good or hard, and without judging it, trace it the way you'd follow a river from its source. Then rest in the breath alone.
Shapa, a curse: the sage Kindama's dying words to the king whose arrow struck him in a moment of love.
Your line: you've killed me in a moment of love. One arrow, and a king's future changed. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Ahimsa, not harming living beings, is an important value in Hindu traditions, and stories like Kindama's are retold to show how seriously a harm, even in a lawful hunt, can be taken.

give up the royal life and live as an ascetic.

chat.says: Why did Pandu leave his throne and go live as an ascetic?
options: A dying sage he'd shot cursed him, so he could never father a son.
He lost a war, and the Kuru elders sent him away to the forest.
Dhritarashtra asked for the crown, and Pandu gave it up gladly.
chat.meaning: Pandu shot the sage Kindama in a deer's form. The dying sage's curse meant he could have no sons, so he left the royal life.

Kunti.meaning: Pandu's first wife, who chose him at her self-choice

Kuntibhoja.meaning: the king who raised Kunti as his daughter

Kindama.meaning: the sage in a deer's form who cursed Pandu

Brahmanas.meaning: priests and scholars, the priestly class

recall: gods cursed to be born as men

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva (Kunti's self-choice; Madri; Pandu's conquests and retreat to the forest; the sage Kindama's curse; Pandu's resolve)
